quests.scene: Your team has strongly conflicting ideas on how to approach a critical and time-sensitive project.
options: Simply adopt the idea of the most experienced person.
Take a vote on which approach to follow.
Facilitate a structured discussion where each approach is evaluated against agreed criteria before any decision is made.
Let the conflict eventually resolve on its own.
quests.hint: Agreed criteria remove personality and status from decision-making entirely.
quests.explanation: Agreeing on evaluation criteria first makes decisions more objective and earns genuine team buy-in.

quests.scene: You need to give performance feedback to someone who is twice your age about their communication style.
options: Avoid the conversation entirely.
Apologise throughout the entire conversation.
I value your experience enormously. I wanted to share something I've heard from others in the team - with the sincere goal of making your communication even more effective.
Tell them directly and bluntly what needs to change.
quests.hint: Acknowledge their experience and frame feedback as amplifying their already genuine effectiveness.
quests.explanation: Honouring their experience and framing the feedback as third-party observations in service of their effectiveness is both respectful and credible.

quests.scene: You are about to have a very difficult conversation with a colleague who tends to become highly defensive.
options: Be completely blunt - soft approaches simply do not work with this person.
Soften the message so much that the real point is completely lost.
Open with genuine recognition: I want to start by saying I truly value what you bring. This conversation comes from that honest place.
Ask someone else to have the conversation for you.
quests.hint: Opening with genuine recognition significantly reduces defensiveness before your message lands.
quests.explanation: Establishing positive intent and authentic appreciation before the challenging message creates psychological safety.

quests.scene: You are leading a significant change in an organisation where many people are deeply resistant.
options: Push the change through regardless of the resistance.
Give up and simply accept the resistance as final.
Actively engage the resistors early: I'd like to understand your specific concerns - they may genuinely improve how we implement this.
Implement the changes quietly and secretly without involving people.
quests.hint: Resistors often hold genuinely valuable insights. Engage them early and proactively.
quests.explanation: Inviting resistance as input is both strategically smart and deeply respectful. People consistently support what they have genuinely helped to create.

quests.scene: You notice a consistent pattern of gender bias in how contributions are acknowledged at meetings.
options: Say nothing - it is not your place to raise this.
Call out the bias aggressively and publicly in front of everyone.
Raise the pattern privately with the meeting organiser: I've noticed something I think is worth reflecting on - would you be open to a brief conversation about it?
File a formal complaint immediately without any prior conversation.
quests.hint: Raise observed systemic issues at the appropriate level and always in private first.
quests.explanation: A private conversation with the organiser framed as worth reflecting on is the right first step.

quests.scene: Your company culture has become genuinely toxic but you love the actual work. What matters most when deciding to stay or leave?
options: The salary is always the only truly relevant factor.
The quality of the work must override everything else.
Weigh the long-term personal cost to your wellbeing against the short-term professional reward - culture profoundly affects health growth and long-term career trajectory.
Stay until you happen to find something better elsewhere.
quests.hint: Culture directly shapes your health your professional growth and your entire career trajectory.
quests.explanation: A thorough evaluation of genuine wellbeing costs weighed against professional rewards with careful attention to long-term career impact is the mature strategic approach.

quests.scene: You want to ask for a professional reference from someone you have not spoken to in over two years.
options: Email them directly: Can I use you as a reference?
Simply list their name without asking their permission.
Reconnect first with a genuine personal update and then make the reference request after re-establishing contact.
Ask someone else entirely without informing them.
quests.hint: Re-establish the human relationship before making any professional request.
quests.explanation: Reconnecting genuinely before asking for the favour is both more respectful and more practically effective.

quests.scene: You are presenting complex financial data to a board that includes both financial and non-financial members.
options: Present the complete data in full - board members should understand it.
Simplify so dramatically that key nuances are entirely lost.
Layer the presentation: lead with the story behind the numbers present headline figures and offer full technical detail as an appendix for those who want it.
Outsource the financial presentation section to someone else.
quests.hint: Layered communication serves genuinely mixed audiences far better than any single approach.
quests.explanation: Story first headlines second technical detail as optional depth serves every audience member at their own level.

quests.scene: Your mentor asks you directly: What kind of support are you actually looking for from me?
options: Whatever you happen to be able to offer.
General guidance and advice on my career.

I'd find it most valuable to have a regular sounding board specifically for strategic decisions particularly around [specific area] - and to have someone who will challenge my thinking when I'm too close to a problem.
Professional introductions and network connections.
quests.hint: Specific actionable requests make mentoring relationships dramatically more productive.
quests.explanation: A specific honest answer gives the mentor clear and useful direction and signals genuine self-awareness about what you need.

quests.scene: You are leading a post-mortem review after a significant project failure.
options: Focus primarily on identifying which individuals made which mistakes.
Move through it as quickly as possible.
Create a psychologically safe environment where the team can discuss honestly what went wrong - without blame - and identify the systemic lessons.
Share only the positive learnings from the experience.
quests.hint: Post-mortems need genuine psychological safety to produce honest and useful insights.
quests.explanation: A blameless post-mortem creates the conditions for real honesty. Systemic issues not individuals are the most valuable outputs.

quests.scene: You receive a LinkedIn recommendation that praises you but contains a significant factual inaccuracy.
options: Accept it gratefully - more positive content is always better.
Ask them to remove it entirely.
Reach out privately: I truly appreciate this - could I suggest one small factual adjustment? I want it to be as accurate and credible as possible.
Ignore the inaccuracy - it is not important.
quests.hint: Inaccurate professional praise can ultimately undermine your credibility and set expectations you cannot meet.
quests.explanation: Asking for an adjustment framed as wanting accuracy ensures the recommendation is genuinely credible.

quests.scene: You need to write a compelling internal email to senior leadership requesting budget for a new strategic initiative.
options: Begin by explaining how much budget you are requesting.
Focus on the personal and team benefits the initiative would bring.
Frame the request clearly around business impact: the specific problem being solved the expected return on investment and the resources required.
Keep the tone deliberately informal and personal.
quests.hint: Budget requests must speak the precise language of business impact.
quests.explanation: Problem being solved + expected business return + resources required is the fundamental structure of any compelling internal budget request.

quests.scene: You are in a creative brainstorming session and a colleague says: That idea will never work.
options: Defend your idea passionately and immediately.
Drop the idea entirely and move to the next one.
Ask: What is your main concern with it? I'd genuinely like to understand where the gap is.
Tell them to be more open to creative thinking.
quests.hint: Ask why before either defending or abandoning any idea.
quests.explanation: Asking what is your main concern? turns an objection into useful information and keeps the creative process genuinely open.

quests.scene: You are asked to set meaningful performance KPIs for your team for the coming year.
options: Copy the KPIs from a comparable department.
Set them top-down without involving your team.
Set KPIs collaboratively ensuring they are specific genuinely measurable and clearly aligned with the company's overall strategic direction.
Use purely quantitative metrics exclusively.
quests.hint: Collaborative strategic and measurable KPIs consistently work better than imposed ones.
quests.explanation: Collaborative KPI-setting increases team ownership and commitment.

quests.scene: You are leading a global team and need to run a genuinely effective first kickoff meeting.
options: Assume your own communication norms apply equally to all cultures.
Focus exclusively on the project deliverables and timeline.
Begin with introductions that go beyond roles - include what each person uniquely contributes and what they personally hope to achieve. Then set shared working norms and actively invite input.
Keep it very short to minimise the risk of cultural misunderstandings.
quests.hint: Cross-cultural kickoffs require significant additional investment in relationships and shared norms.
quests.explanation: Introductions beyond formal roles explicitly shared working norms and deliberately inclusive participation from the very start create the psychological foundation for high-performing global teams.

quests.scene: A colleague accuses you of having a conflict of interest in a decision you were involved in.
options: Deny it immediately and strongly.
Become visibly defensive.
Thank them for raising it acknowledge any possible appearance of conflict transparently and offer to recuse yourself from the relevant decision if appropriate.
Tell them it is genuinely none of their business.
quests.hint: Conflict of interest concerns deserve complete transparency - not defensiveness.
quests.explanation: Thanking them honestly acknowledging the potential appearance of conflict and offering recusal demonstrates genuine professional integrity.

quests.scene: You are onboarding a new team member entirely remotely. How do you ensure they feel genuinely included?
options: Send them the company handbook and onboarding documents.
Have your manager handle the entire onboarding process.
Assign a dedicated buddy schedule regular short check-in calls proactively introduce them to key people and deliberately over-communicate in their first few weeks.
Wait for them to ask questions and reach out when they need something.
quests.hint: Remote onboarding requires deliberate structured and sustained inclusion efforts.
quests.explanation: A buddy plus regular check-ins plus proactive introductions plus intentional over-communication are the key ingredients of successful remote onboarding.

quests.scene: You are asked for your personal view on a significant ethical workplace dilemma in a room full of senior colleagues.
options: Share your strongest instinctive opinion immediately and confidently.
Stay completely vague to avoid any possible controversy.
Take a brief moment then respond: This involves genuinely competing values that I take seriously. Let me share my reasoning and the key tensions I see. Then offer a clearly reasoned position.
Say you need significantly more time to think before commenting.
quests.hint: Demonstrating your reasoning process is as important as the position you ultimately take.
quests.explanation: Showing the real tensions between competing values before landing on a clear position demonstrates intellectual depth.

quests.scene: You have worked for weeks on a technical document and your editor says it needs to be completely rewritten.
options: Reject the feedback - you have invested too much to change everything.
Rewrite it precisely as suggested even if you privately disagree.
This is genuinely hard to hear but I want to fully understand your reasoning before I respond. Can you walk me through your main concerns with it?
Send it immediately to a second editor for their view.
quests.hint: Fully absorb difficult editorial feedback before you respond to it.
quests.explanation: Asking to understand the reasoning before reacting is emotionally mature. It prevents a defensive response you may later regret.

quests.scene: You need to explain to a senior stakeholder why your project has significantly exceeded its budget.
options: Blame exclusively external factors beyond your control.
Hope that they simply do not ask about it.
Present a clear honest account: We are over budget by [X] due to [specific and honest reason]. Here is what we learned and here is our specific revised plan for the remainder.
Focus entirely on the aspects of the project that went well.
quests.hint: Own the overrun fully explain the genuine cause and immediately present your plan.
quests.explanation: A specific honest account with a clear cause and a credible revised plan is more professionally credible than any denial or deflection.

quests.scene: You are designing a comprehensive communication strategy for a major internal organisational restructuring.
options: Send one clear email from leadership and consider the communication done.
Make a single major town hall announcement and take no further questions.

Use a multi-channel staged approach: leadership message followed by manager briefings dedicated Q and A sessions and ongoing structured updates with specific tailored messaging for each affected group.
Say as little as publicly possible about the change.
quests.hint: Complex organisational change always requires staged targeted multi-channel communication.
quests.explanation: A multi-channel audience-segmented approach addresses the informational and emotional needs of each group affected by the change.

quests.scene: You are presenting a new strategic direction to an audience you know is genuinely sceptical.
options: Begin with your most compelling data slide.
Open by directly acknowledging the scepticism: I know some of you have real concerns about this direction. I want to address those head-on right from the start.
Dive straight into your strategic plan.
Begin by thoroughly explaining why the previous approach failed.
quests.hint: Address real resistance explicitly at the beginning - not at the end.
quests.explanation: Naming scepticism upfront creates genuine psychological openness. Trying to sell strategy to unaddressed sceptics with data alone almost never works effectively.

quests.scene: You discover your team is duplicating significant work that another department has already completed.
options: Let them finish - it is too late in the process to change anything.
Tell your team directly that all their work was unnecessary.
Connect with the other department to understand what already exists then redirect your team's energy toward the genuine gaps that remain.
Blame the organisational communication structures for the overlap.
quests.hint: Turn discovered duplication into a real cross-team collaboration opportunity.
quests.explanation: Connecting departments to share what already exists and redirecting effort to genuine gaps is constructive and also builds valuable relationships across organisational silos.

quests.scene: You are running a workshop and can feel that the energy in the room has dropped significantly.
options: Push on with the planned agenda regardless.
End the workshop significantly early.
I can feel the energy is low right now - let's take a short five-minute break and come back with fresh eyes and renewed focus.
Simply increase your own visible energy level to try to compensate.
quests.hint: Naming what the room is genuinely experiencing is more effective than ignoring or performing around it.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging low energy and taking a break resets the group far more effectively than pushing through.

quests.scene: You are reviewing your company's diversity hiring practices and the data clearly shows they are falling well short.
options: Blame the external pipeline - qualified candidates simply do not exist.
Ignore the data and carry on.
Present the findings honestly then facilitate a structured stage-by-stage review of where the drop-off is occurring and what specific actions will address each stage.
Implement a quick superficial cosmetic fix.
quests.hint: Systemic hiring problems require rigorous systemic analysis and carefully staged solutions.
quests.explanation: Honest data plus stage-by-stage analysis of where in the process the drop-off occurs plus specific interventions for each stage is the only rigorous and effective approach.

quests.scene: Your direct report tells you they are being consistently undermined by a senior colleague.
options: Confront the senior colleague directly without speaking to your report first.
Tell your report to deal with it themselves.
Listen carefully to the full account believe them provisionally and then work out the most appropriate response together with them.
Dismiss the concern as likely interpersonal sensitivity.
quests.hint: Support your report by listening fully and actively involving them in how you respond.
quests.explanation: Listening carefully believing provisionally and co-creating the response empowers the employee while ensuring the situation is handled appropriately.

quests.scene: You are writing a funding application for a significant project. What is the single most important element?
options: A professionally designed and beautiful layout.
A comprehensive and detailed list of all your planned activities.
A clear and compelling case for why your project addresses a specific real-world need and what measurable impact it will have.
Extensive evidence of your organisation's past history and credentials.
quests.hint: Funders invest in demonstrated impact - not in activities or organisational history.
quests.explanation: Specific need plus measurable impact is the core of every effective funding application.

quests.scene: A key team member with critical knowledge announces they are resigning. They leave in two weeks.
options: Offer them anything to get them to stay.
Accept the resignation and do nothing further.
Immediately plan a comprehensive knowledge transfer: identify exactly what critical knowledge exists schedule intensive transfer sessions and systematically document everything before their last day.
Focus on quickly replacing them rather than transferring their knowledge first.
quests.hint: Structured knowledge transfer must begin immediately when any critical person announces departure.
quests.explanation: A systematic knowledge transfer protected the team and organisation. The goal is to make knowledge institutional rather than leaving it personal and irreplaceable.

quests.scene: You are drafting a crisis communication message after your company issues a product recall.
options: Minimise the significance of the problem in your communication.
Say as little as possible to limit reputational damage.
Acknowledge the issue clearly and directly take explicit responsibility explain precisely what is being done and provide a clear specific action for customers to take.
Publicly blame the supplier for the defect.
quests.hint: Crisis communication requires immediate clarity genuine responsibility and specific customer actions.
quests.explanation: Clear acknowledgment plus explicit responsibility plus corrective action plus clear customer guidance is the four-part structure of effective crisis communication.

quests.scene: Your senior leadership team is genuinely divided on the company's strategic direction. You are facilitating.
options: Ask the CEO to simply make the final decision.
Put the options to a vote.
Use a structured decision-making process: first align clearly on the criteria for a good strategic decision then evaluate each option against those agreed criteria.
Let the disagreement remain unresolved.
quests.hint: Strategic disagreements at the leadership level need structured process - not hierarchical override.
quests.explanation: Agreeing on decision criteria first removes both ego and rank from the evaluation process and consistently produces more defensible team-owned strategic decisions.
